original_question: Given n points in space with no four coplanar, determine the largest integer m for which one can guarantee that some m of the n points are the vertices of a convex polyhedron.
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 in Section 1, specialized to d = 3, together with the introductory definition of ES_d(n), general position, and convex position.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the 3-dimensional setting, the general-position condition in that setting ('no four coplanar'), and the target configuration as a subset that forms the vertex set of a convex polyhedron.
missing_details: The paper does not phrase the problem as 'given n points, find the largest guaranteed m'; it introduces the threshold function ES_d(n), the smallest integer N such that every N-point set in R^d in general position contains n points in convex position.
The ambient space should be stated explicitly as Euclidean 3-space R^3.

The official notion is 'in convex position'; in R^3 this means that every selected point is a vertex of the convex hull of the selected set, equivalently the selected set is the vertex set of a convex polyhedron.
The quantifiers must be explicit: for every integer t, every set of ES_3(t) points in general position in R^3 contains a t-point subset in convex position.
The paper's nearest official formulation is asymptotic, not exact finite determination: it conjectures the order of growth of ES_d(n), not an exact formula for the inverse guarantee function.

If one specializes Conjecture 1.1 to d = 3, the statement must include the asymptotic meaning of 2^{Theta(sqrt(t))}: there exist constants c, C > 0 such that 2^{c sqrt(t)} <= ES_3(t) <= 2^{C sqrt(t)} for all sufficiently large t.

Your variables are role-reversed relative to the paper: your n is the total number of given points, whereas the paper uses n for the desired convex-position subset size and ES_3(n) for the required total number of points.
refined_question: For each integer t >= 1, let ES_3(t) denote the smallest integer N such that every set of N points in Euclidean 3-space R^3 in general position (that is, with no four points coplanar) contains a t-point subset in convex position, equivalently, t points that are the vertices of a convex polyhedron. Is it true that ES_3(t) = 2^{Theta(sqrt(t))} as t -> infinity?
justification: The supplied identifier math/0010143 resolves on arXiv to an unrelated number-theory paper, 'Thirty-Six Unsolved Problems in Number Theory', whereas your draft and your instruction to prioritize Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, and Theorem 1.3 match Mubayi-Suk, 'The Erdős-Szekeres problem and an induced Ramsey question.' ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0010143)) In that paper, the geometric object is the higher-dimensional Erdős-Szekeres threshold ES_d(n): the minimum number of points in R^d in general position needed to force an n-point subset in convex position; Conjecture 1.1 predicts ES_d(n) = 2^{Theta(n^{1/(d-1)})} for every d >= 3. Specializing to d = 3 gives exactly the sharp, stand-alone question above. Proposition 1.2 provides the induced-hypergraph reformulation via Motzkin's 0/2/4 phenomenon, and Theorem 1.3 supplies evidence by proving a strong lower bound for the associated induced Ramsey number. ([mathweb.ucsd.edu](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~asuk/ESinduced_072818v2.pdf?utm_source=openai))
